verses.translation_literal: A psalm of David. YHWH, who will sojourn in your tent? Who will dwell on your mountain of holiness?
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm, of David. LORD, who may be a guest in your tent? Who may settle on the mountain that is yours and holy?
verses.directors_commentary: This is an entrance liturgy: pilgrims stand at the gate and ask what it takes to come in. Play it as a real question put to a real doorkeeper, with the crowd listening. The two verbs are not synonyms. Yagur is the verb for the ger, the resident outsider with no land or family of his own, who lives under someone else's protection; shakhan is to settle and pitch one's own tent. The question is who may be received as a guest of YHWH and who may stay. The KJV's 'abide' for the first verb loses the guest-and-stranger sense, and 'tabernacle' is an archaism where the Hebrew has the plain word 'ohel, tent. The tent is a shelter and a household: hospitality law meant that whoever ate under a host's roof was under his protection. The mountain of holiness is Zion, where David had pitched a tent for the ark (2 Samuel 6:17). Ibn Ezra reads it as Moriah or Zion, Radak as Moriah, and Radak also hears heaven in 'tent'. The KJV renders 'mountain of your holiness' as 'thy holy hill', which turns a noun into an adjective and shrinks a mountain to a hill. The Hebrew says 'the mountain of your holiness': the holiness belongs to YHWH and the mountain is only where it is found.

philological_notes.note: From gur 'to sojourn', the verb of the ger, a resident alien who lives under a host's protection. Here the guest of YHWH's tent. Distinct from shakhan, 'to settle'.
A tent, here the sanctuary as YHWH's household. Ibn Ezra glosses it simply as 'your house'; Radak takes it as the heavens, stretched out like a tent.

verses.translation_literal: Walking blameless, and doing righteousness, and speaking truth in his heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: The one who walks without blemish. The one whose hands do what is right. The one who speaks the truth, and speaks it first inside his own heart, where no one hears.
verses.directors_commentary: The answer comes at once and without a verb of its own: three participles in a row, a description rather than a rule. Hear a steady beat, walking, doing, speaking, a whole life in three words. Tamim is not 'perfect' but whole, without a missing part, the word used for an unblemished sacrificial animal; the KJV's 'uprightly' turns a quality of the person into a manner of walking, and the ASV and BBE follow it. Ibn Ezra reads it as a shortened 'walking in the way of the blameless'. Tzedek is conduct that fits the relationship at hand: fairness to the person in front of you. The last line is the surprise. The truth is spoken 'in his heart', and the KJV's 'speaketh the truth in his heart' keeps the words but not the weight. In Hebrew thought the lev is the seat of thought and will, so the speaker is truthful in private deliberation. Rashi reads it as one whose mouth and heart agree, and Radak adds that he keeps what he resolved in his heart. Let the actor drop the voice here. Malbim hears a ladder in the three clauses: conduct toward God (blameless, everything done for God alone), toward the neighbor (doing righteousness), and inward faith (truth in the heart, belief that is not only on the lips). Meiri reads it differently: blameless means humble, not proud of his deeds even as he does righteousness, and truth in the heart means that heart and mouth agree in everything.

philological_notes.note: Whole, complete, without defect; used of unblemished offerings. The moral sense is integrity, not flawlessness. Radak notes it can be an adjective ('walking a blameless way') or a noun ('walking in blamelessness').

'In his heart': the inner place where thought and decision happen. The truth is told there first. Rashi: the good he says in his heart is true, and he is not one thing with the mouth and another in the heart.

verses.translation_literal: He has not gone about on his tongue; he has not done evil to his companion; and reproach he has not lifted up against his near one.
verses.translation_dramatic: His tongue has never gone out on foot through the neighbors' lanes. He has done his friend no harm. And when shame comes to the door of someone close to him, he does not pick it up and carry it from house to house.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the answer turns to what he does not do, and the grammar changes: three perfects with 'not', each a closed door. Ragal is the verb to watch. It comes from regel, 'foot', so the slanderer is one whose tongue goes about on foot, a gossip peddling his news from door to door, a spy. Rashi and Ibn Ezra tie it to the same verb in 2 Samuel 19:28, where Mephibosheth says Ziba 'slandered' his servant to David, and Ibn Ezra adds that the sense is revealing secrets, as spies do. The KJV's 'backbiteth' is a good old word but it drops the image of feet. Hear the walk in the sound: ragal 'al leshono. Then a second play of sound: ra'ah, evil, done le-re'ehu, to his companion; the two words share the consonants r-'-h, so harm done to a friend is a betrayal built into the sounds. In a village where everyone lives within sight of everyone, reputation was a form of property and a shared water supply. The last clause is hard. Nasa' kherpah is literally 'to lift up reproach': the KJV's 'taketh up a reproach' is close, but the phrase can mean to pick up and pass on a slur, or to bring shame on one's kin. Rashi reads it as one who punishes a relative's offense rather than covering it up, so that no enemy can say 'your relative did this and you shielded him'. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri give other readings, and the BBE's 'take away the good name' is a guess. The KJV's repeated 'neighbour' flattens two Hebrew words, re'a and qarov, near one.

philological_notes.note: A verb made from regel 'foot': to go about on foot, to spy, hence to slander. The same verb occurs in 2 Samuel 19:28. Metzudat Zion and Rashi gloss it as spreading gossip and slander.

Reproach, taunt, shame. With nasa' 'to lift up' it is the act of taking up a slur: to bring it, bear it or pass it on. Radak compares nasa' with the verb in 'you shall not lift up the name of YHWH to emptiness' and 'you shall not lift up a false report'.
'His near one': a relative or someone near to him. Radak treats it as a synonym of re'a, a neighbor close in business and dealings. Rashi reads it as a kinsman, whose sin he does not shield.

verses.translation_literal: Despised in his eyes, a rejected one; but those who fear YHWH he honors. He swears to do harm [to himself] and does not change.
verses.translation_dramatic: In his eyes the rejected man is small and he is despised. But the ones who fear the LORD he lifts up and honors. And if he has sworn an oath that costs him dearly, he does not take it back.
verses.directors_commentary: Two portraits meet in one line, and the staging is a matter of where this man looks. His eyes find the one who is rejected and he sees contempt-worthy, then they travel to the God-fearers and he gives them weight. Kavod, honor, is literally 'heaviness', so he gives the right people weight and the wrong people none. The KJV's 'a vile person is contemned' reads nivzeh and nim'as as one man's description: 'vile', 'contemned'. But both words are passive participles of rejection, 'despised' and 'rejected', and no noun is attached. The ASV and KJV both treat the despised as another person; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri hear a man humble in his own eyes. The BBE's 'turning away from him who has not the Lord's approval' is an interpretation. The oath clause is the hardest to read aloud: nishba' lehara' wela yamir, 'sworn to do harm, and does not change'. The KJV supplies 'his own' in italics, as Rashi does ('to himself'), and Radak reads it as an oath to fast or give away for a good cause. Yamir is the verb of exchange: he does not swap the oath for something easier. Oaths in a village were binding, public and invoked the deity, so breaking one drew down more than embarrassment. Let the actor choose which harm; the Hebrew leaves it open.

philological_notes.note: Two Niphal participles, 'despised' and 'rejected', with no noun. The usual reading is a contemptible person whom the righteous man scorns; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri hear instead a man who counts himself small.
Hiphil infinitive 'to do harm, to hurt'. The Hebrew has no 'his own'; Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all supply a harm to himself, such as fasting.
Hiphil of mur, 'to exchange, change'. Metzudat Zion: from temurah, 'exchange, substitution'. He does not trade the oath for another.

verses.translation_literal: His silver he has not given for interest, and a bribe against the innocent he has not taken. The doer of these will not be shaken for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: His silver he has never lent out to feed on the borrower. And no gift in the hand has ever bought his word against a man who is clean. Whoever lives like this will not be shaken. Not now, and not ever.
verses.directors_commentary: The list ends in money, as most such lists do, with two clauses of what he does not do and then a promise. Neshekh is literally 'a bite', from the verb nashakh, to bite: interest that eats the borrower. The KJV's 'usury' belongs to a later world of bankers; Israel's law forbade interest on a loan to a poor countryman (Exodus 22:24, Leviticus 25:36), and in a subsistence farm economy a loan was usually a lifeline after a bad harvest, so interest meant a path from debt to losing the land and ending as a slave. Radak, writing with an eye on debates of his own time, argues that the law forbids this only between Israelites. The second clause is a courtroom: the elders judged at the gate, and a shohad, a gift pressed into the judge's hand, was forbidden because it blinds. The bribe is taken 'against the innocent', so the verb is lakach, to take, and it is the judge's hand that closes. Rashi gives two readings: a bribe to condemn the poor man, or, as the Sifre has it, not even a bribe to acquit the innocent. The last line is a promise in the image of a building: 'will not be shaken' (yimmot), as a house on rock does not totter. 'For ever' is le'olam, not only in this life; Radak hears the afterlife here. The KJV's 'shall never be moved' is accurate; its 'putteth out his money' is not what the Hebrew says. The Hebrew says simply 'give', natan, and it says 'silver', kesef: silver weighed out by the shekel, not coin, which Israel did not yet strike in David's day.

philological_notes.note: 'Interest', literally a bite, from nashakh 'to bite'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as ribbit. The law bans it on loans to a poor fellow Israelite.

A bribe, a gift to a judge or official. Rashi gives two readings: against the poor man to condemn him, or on behalf of the innocent to clear him, and then argues a fortiori that he would not take one to bend a judgment.
Niphal of mot, 'to totter, to be shaken'. The image is of a house or foundation giving way. Rashi: even if he is shaken, he rises again.
